doc.title: Loren Schoenberg interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2019

chapter: Manhattan School of Music and Eddie Durham
title: Sitting in with Francis Williams and Eddie Durham; Goshen gig
summary: He sits in with Williams and Durham, then plays in Durham's quartet in Goshen, NY for years.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: Wilder. In other words classically trained, read flyspecks, and even more than Joe, he was different than Joe, he was not the soloist, the great personal soloist that Joe was. He played great, fine solos. But he was like a Snooky Young or Al Killian or he was like a dynamite lead player. And he had a band with Eddie Durham. And I was so desperate to sit in with him I just took out my saxophone one night and, during a break, to show them like that I wasn’t going to muck it up, and I played a little and they said okay you can sit in. And this began a long association with Eddie Durham that was profound for me on many, many levels — musically but also fifty percent culturally. And so what happened was while I was at Manhattan School of Music switching to saxophone major, some great musicians were around there: Ted Rosenthal was in school, a guy named Roy Gerson, Manny Mendelson, other names will come back to me — some really, really fine players were in school at that time. You mentioned about studying before going to college, college before college. Well this was even more. So Eddie Durham had a quartet and I wound up playing in his quartet in a small town up in the Catskills called Goshen, New York, Exit 124 off of Route 6 and Route 17. And I wound up playing there for years, maybe three or four years with him on the weekends. So his band was all people like him, older musicians, a drummer named Harold Austin, who had been the drummer with Jonah Jones’s quartet and had been in Harlem since the 30s, a wonderful piano player named Kelly Owens who was on Big Maybelle and those early like, early R&Bish kind of records, and there I was this little kid, 18, 19, but playing night after night after long set after long set, just exposed to these sounds. I mean Eddie Durham was the guy who created, you know, the modern Benny Moten band and the Count Basie band and I mean in terms of the arrangements. And he was also a pioneer on the electric guitar, and he played the electric guitar in that band too. And so just to wrap this one thing up, but the other part of it, besides the music was, and this gets back to another early question of yours about sociological versus musicological. Here I am an 18-year-old kid Jewish kid from the suburbs, and I’m being welcomed into this world of these African-American musicians who are sixty and seventy and who they’re staying with, and how people treat one another, and all I can say is like I was so — I mean I could get very emotional now and I’m not going to, but they were so warm and loving and accepting and encouraging in every way that I experienced something about a world that like I didn’t know about. It wasn’t like my world, not to put my world down. And I used to think all the time about the inverse — well meaning white liberal people who might take in someone as I was to them into their midst and wrap their arms around them. I don’t think it would have been the same. I don’t think it would have been the same. And as I got older and started to reflect after decades and years about all those things and what those people went through and what their lives were like and the great joys and satisfactions.
